rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient at mid temperature to reveal the full elution window and avoid truncation. This should show whether any compounds are unretained early or still eluting near the end, guiding later narrowing of the gradient window and slope tuning.

All pairs are already fully resolved, so the objective is now to cut retention time while keeping resolution above 1.5. The first run suggests the peaks occupy only a middle portion of the solvent range, so a narrower, steeper window with higher temperature should pull the last peak closer to 10 minutes without risking truncation.

We already have the maximum CRF, so now probe whether the method can be shortened further while keeping the weakest pair above 1.5. This keeps the successful window and temperature fixed and tests a steeper gradient as the cleanest next optimization step.

Resolution is still comfortably above threshold, so continue shortening the gradient along the same window to find the fastest method before the first pair drops below 1.5. The limiting pair remains peaks 1 and 2, making this the most direct boundary test.

At tG 4 min the weakest pair is still above 1.5, so test the shortest allowed gradient to see if full resolution is preserved. This is the quickest way to locate the lower time limit on the successful method family.

The shortest gradient failed only for the first pair, and that pair is eluting very early, so lowering phi0 should give them more initial retention and recover margin without lengthening the run too much. Keeping tG at 4 min starts from the fastest fully successful method and tests whether the window can be shifted to improve robustness.

Lowering phi0 restored margin for the first pair at 4 min, so now retest the 2 min gradient with that improved starting strength. This directly checks whether the extra early retention is enough to make the shortest method fully resolved.

The only failing pair is still the earliest one, so push phi0 to the lowest allowed value while keeping the 2 min gradient to maximize initial focusing and retention of peaks 1 and 2. This tests whether further lowering the starting strength can rescue the shortest method without sacrificing the fast last peak.

The first pair is slope-sensitive and remains the limiting pair, so test a lower temperature to add retention and potentially improve selectivity while staying with the fastest fully successful gradient shape. This checks whether temperature can create more margin than the 50 C method without giving up full resolution.

Lowering temperature improved the limiting first pair at 4 min, so now test whether that selectivity gain is enough to make the 2 min gradient fully resolved. This is the key experiment to see if temperature, rather than window changes, can unlock the shortest method.

The 2 min method improved markedly when temperature dropped from 50 to 45 C, so continue in that direction to see if the limiting first pair can cross the 1.5 threshold. This isolates temperature as the tuning variable while keeping the fastest gradient unchanged.

The 2 min method is now just below the full-resolution threshold, and the monotonic gain in the first pair with lower temperature suggests one more 5 C drop may succeed. This is the most direct test of whether the shortest allowed gradient can achieve CRF 1.000.

Now that the 2 min method is fully resolved, test whether trimming the high-organic end can pull the last compound slightly earlier while keeping all peaks within the gradient. The last peak still elutes after the programmed gradient, so a modestly lower phi1 is the key boundary check for preserving full resolution with minimal run time.

Lowering phi1 made the last peak much slower, showing the sixth compound is sensitive to the hold composition, so test a slightly higher phi1 to shorten the tail while keeping the same successful 2 min, 35 C framework. This may retain full resolution and reduce the already excellent run time further.

At phi1 0.70 the 2 min method is still fully resolved and much faster than at 0.65, but the first pair is now near the threshold, so test one more increase in phi1 to find the upper boundary before resolution fails. This directly probes whether the run can be shortened further while maintaining CRF 1.000.

Since phi1 0.75 was just too strong for the first pair, keep the favorable high phi1 region but lower temperature one step to gain selectivity and recover resolution. This tests whether a 2 min method can be both fully resolved and even faster than the current phi1 0.70, 35 C result.

Lowering temperature to 30 C restored good margin at phi1 0.70, so now revisit phi1 0.75 under these cooler conditions to see if the faster elution can be retained without losing the first-pair resolution. This is the most promising route to a faster fully resolved 2 min method.

The 2 min method at phi1 0.75 and 30 C is fully resolved with some remaining margin on the first pair, so test one more step higher in phi1 to see if an even faster fully resolved method is possible. This is the natural boundary search from the current best-speed condition.

The current fastest fully resolved method still has a small margin on the first pair, so test one final step higher in phi1 to locate the true upper limit. If resolution remains at or above 1.5, this should further shorten the last peak and define the fastest successful condition so far.

Phi1 0.85 was slightly too aggressive, so keep the successful phi1 0.80 setting and lower temperature one step to increase margin on the critical first pair. This checks whether the fastest fully resolved region can be made more robust while staying very short.

Cooling to 25 C increased the margin at phi1 0.80, so revisit phi1 0.85 under these cooler conditions to see if the faster method can now remain fully resolved. This is the most likely path to the fastest valid method within the tested design space.

The current fastest valid method at phi1 0.85 still has a small but real margin on the critical first pair, so test one final increase in phi1 to search for the absolute fastest fully resolved condition. This is the logical boundary check with the remaining budget.

At phi1 0.90 the first pair missed full credit by only 0.01, suggesting the boundary is controlled almost entirely by the earliest separation; increasing phi0 should reduce the effective gradient span and can improve that pair’s spacing while keeping the very fast high-end elution. This probes whether the current near-optimal high-phi1 method can be nudged back above the threshold with minimal loss in speed.

Raising phi0 to 0.20 unexpectedly improved the limiting first pair while keeping the run very fast, so now combine that with phi1 0.90 to test whether the near-miss at injection 22 can be converted into a fully resolved and even faster method. This is the highest-likelihood route to the fastest CRF 1.000 condition.

With one injection left, push the same high-phi1 fast method by increasing phi0 another step; the last run showed comfortable margin on the critical first pair and the earlier phi0 increase improved rather than hurt it. This is the best remaining chance to find an even faster fully resolved endpoint while staying on the established optimum ridge.
